items.title: Joe Wilder Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: I went to Russia with Benny for the State Department.

ctx.x: It’s so fascinating to think that at that time the music you were playing is like the rock ‘n roll of today. It was the popular music.

At that time it was, yes it was, it was quite popular. And another thing, people listened to a lot of your recordings so that when you went to a town to play, if you had a few recordings out they had listened to them and they knew every note, certainly of the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

ensemble playing you know, and some of the solos, if you repeated them the same way each time, they could hum them note for — or sing them note for note you know. That was true with Benny Goodman and all the big bands at that time.

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When did you start playing with Benny Goodman? ... 1962.

ctx.x: There was enough room for everybody at that point.

Um-hmm. Yeah. And when you consider that during that period – the ’30s and the ’40s – there were so many bands. There were bands on the West Coast, just so many different orchestras. As I say, you could almost – you could identify almost every one of them: Tommy Dorsey, Jimmy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, Fletcher Henderson, Chick Webb, Don Redman. It goes on and on. Gus Arnheim, Andy Kirk. You stop and you say, my goodness, how many of them were there?
What I find interesting too is that the musicians seem to float between one band and another too. There was a lot of movement.
